title: Coach the Skill, Not the Deal: A Conversation with Sandler's Seth Marrs About Sales Coaching That Actually Sticks
summary: What exactly is sales coaching and why do so many organizations think they're doing it when they actually aren't? Get a recap of insights on the coaching consistency gap from Sandler's Seth Marrs.
body_markdown:
Ask almost any sales leader if they value coaching, and the answer is always the same: of course. Ask them how they do it, and a few might have a vague answer. Ask them how they measure it, and you usually get nothing at all.


That gap showed up clearly in Ambition's 2026 State of Sales Coaching Report. 77% of the sales leaders we surveyed said they have a coaching framework, but only 38% reported consistent adoption. Only about 30% said coaching happens weekly or every other week. Nearly half (47%) described their coaching as highly variable or something they can't measure.


I recently sat down with Seth Marrs, Chief Strategy Officer at Sandler, to dig into why that gap exists and what sales leaders can do about it. Seth has spent 25+ years in this space as a practitioner and an analyst, and at Sandler, coaching is foundational to every methodology implementation. Here's what stuck with me.


If you want to watch the full conversation,[check out the recording here.](https://ambition.com/resources/the-coaching-consistency-problem-ambition-sandler-fireside-chat)


## A Deal Review Isn't Coaching


We started with a basic question: what does sales coaching actually mean? It means 30 different things to 30 different people, so it's worth defining.


To me, coaching is a dedicated space where a manager is fully focused on the rep. It's about identifying a skill gap or behavior issue and building a clear plan to close it. It's for the rep, not for the manager.


That's where most teams get tripped up. When I ask customers how they coach, I usually hear about pipeline reviews and deal inspection. Those are important, but they're management, not coaching. A deal review focuses on the *what* : What stage is this in? Is the close date right? Why hasn't it moved? Honestly, it can feel more like an interrogation than development.


Seth framed it in a way I loved. Ask yourself what you're trying to improve. Is it the outcome of this one deal, or the seller's performance across every deal they'll ever work? The real win in coaching is raising the bar for the seller, so every future deal goes better. Deals are a great source of coaching moments, but the goal is a long-term plan for the person.


**Takeaway for sales leaders:** Keep your forecast and pipeline meetings for staging and inspection. Protect your one-on-ones for the skills and behaviors behind the deals. Coach the skill, not the deal.


## Consistency Comes From Structure, Not Good Intentions


Why does coaching fall apart even when leaders believe in it? Seth was refreshingly honest: sales is a short-term game. Miss your number a few quarters in a row and life gets hard, so it's no surprise managers default to whatever is right in front of them.


I see this constantly. A manager plans to work on a rep's development, then hears the day before that a big deal is slipping. The one-on-one turns into a deal review, and the bigger patterns across the pipeline never get addressed.


The fix is a structure simple enough that managers don't have to think about it. At Ambition, we use a framework called CARE:


- **Calendar:** If it's not on the calendar, it doesn't happen. Weekly, bi-weekly, or monthly, just start somewhere.
- **Agenda:** Every one-on-one needs a clear purpose.
- **Rep-led:** Most managers have 7 to 12 direct reports. They can't research every rep before every meeting, so reps should come prepared with the agenda and a self-assessment.
- **Exit with action items:** End with specific next steps and dates, not vague advice. "Send that email" is advice. "Send that email by Thursday and make sure it meets the criteria of the plan" is an action item.


You don't necessarily need software to do this. A shared calendar and a Google Doc work. But you do need the structure, and that's what most teams are missing.


## You Can't Coach What You Can't See


Seth made a strong case that coaching needs a foundation. Telling a rep "good job on that deal" or "bad job on that deal" isn't coaching. You need defined skills, a clear picture of what good looks like, and a way to measure where each seller stands.


At Sandler, they assess sellers on each skill before and after training. That baseline shows exactly where a rep is strong and where they need work. Without it, managers default to coaching whatever they personally think matters most. Seth said that for Sandler-trained teams, that's almost always the[Pain Funnel,](https://go.sandler.com/customgrowth/insights/blog/categories/prospecting-and-qualifying/power-of-the-sandler-pain-funnel/) even when the rep is already great at it and actually struggling with something else.


He compared it to athletes. Twenty years ago, they had to guess where to improve. Today, with visibility into everything, they can target very specific skills. When you can't see what's going on, you guess. When you can, you get targeted.


## AI Makes Coaching Harder, and More Valuable


This was one of my favorite parts of the conversation. A lot of people assume AI will make a manager's job easier. Seth argued the opposite.


In the past, managers could peanut-butter-spread the same advice across the whole team. Now that they have rich data on every rep, they're expected to tailor coaching to the individual. An introvert and an extrovert should execute the same skill differently, and a good coach has to figure out how to make it work for each person. That takes real collaboration.


He also pointed out that AI tends to give you the average of historical best answers. The best coaching advice usually isn't average. It's tailored to a specific person in a specific situation, and that still requires a human who knows the rep.


So where does AI help? Our survey found only 26% of sales leaders are using AI for coaching. I would have guessed closer to 80%, because the use cases are so practical. I think about it in three stages:


1. **Before:** Use AI to gather performance KPIs, pipeline data, and rep context so managers aren't spending an hour building a research project before every one-on-one. Two minutes between meetings should be enough to walk in prepared.
2. **During:** Let an AI notetaker capture the conversation, summarize it, and log the action items both sides agreed to.
3. **After:** Tie the skill gaps you uncovered to assigned work and the next best action for the rep, so the follow-up actually happens.


One more low-hanging opportunity: use AI to analyze calls against your sales methodology. Whether it's BANT, MEDDIC, or Sandler, AI can find patterns across dozens of conversations where a rep is missing a step, instead of relying on one call a manager happened to watch.


**Takeaway for sales leaders:** Let AI handle the context-gathering. Spend the time it saves on the human part: understanding what motivates each rep and how they like to receive feedback.


## Lead With Value Before Visibility


Seth raised a point every leader rolling out call recording or AI tools should hear. Imagine a rep starts recording their calls, and the first conversation they have about it is a list of five things they did wrong. How motivated will they be to keep recording? Suddenly, customers don't want to be recorded and the bot keeps "forgetting" to join.


His advice is to start with value, not criticism. Use these tools first for things that save sellers time, like pre-call prep and post-call follow-up. Once they're part of the daily workflow, coaching follows naturally. Seth predicted that, done right, sellers will start asking managers to listen to their calls and tell them whether they nailed a skill.


Two things have to be true first: the rep has to believe the coaching adds value, and they have to trust that it's in their best interest.


## Measure Coaching by Results, Not Completion


How do you know coaching is working? For a long time, the honest answer was that you didn't. Training completion became the default success metric. Seth argued that's no longer good enough. Enablement has to be a growth driver.


His approach is to pick the three skills you believe will unlock a seller's performance, then watch for that performance to rise in step with those skills over a full sales cycle. His rule of thumb for sizing that cycle: anchor to how often you pay commission. If comp is annual, a one-year development plan is perfectly reasonable, even in a quarter-to-quarter business. Shorter sales cycles will just show evidence sooner, through leading indicators like deal velocity and volume.


He also added an important caveat: be willing to admit you picked the wrong skill. If a rep improves on a skill but results don't move, go back to the drawing board and find the thing that will actually unlock them.


## Two Things You Can Do This Month


We closed by asking for one practical step each.


**Seth's recommendation: build a skills growth plan.** Pick the top three skills that move the needle for your team. Evaluate a handful of calls yourself to baseline where your reps stand. Then coach to those skills, track performance through a full sales cycle, and iterate if you picked the wrong ones.


**My recommendation: run a 30-day reinforcement pilot.** Training doesn't stick without reinforcement. Reps get certified, then fall right back into old habits. So pick one skill and a few managers you trust to commit. Run weekly, structured one-on-ones using the CARE framework, with enablement supporting. Baseline at the start, document action items every week, and measure at the end. If you don't document it and measure it, it won't happen.


## Where Coaching Is Headed


Five or six years ago, recording sales calls seemed like something reps would never accept. Today it's standard practice. I believe the coaching conversation itself is next.


That's why we're launching Coaching Intelligence at Ambition this November. It does three things: builds agentic agendas that pull a rep's performance context into every one-on-one, captures and summarizes the conversation with action items, and rolls coaching themes up so managers, enablement, and leadership can spot patterns across the team. For the first time, organizations can see a real coaching record, not just whether one-on-ones happened.


But the biggest takeaway from my conversation with Seth isn't about technology. As more of the sales cycle gets automated, the seller in the room with the buyer becomes the biggest differentiator. Helping that person become the best seller they can be is still the most important job a manager has.
